title: Iran, Bolivia and Two More Countries Drop Visa-Free Access for Indians as Passport Ranking Slips
excerpt: India falls to 81st on the Henley Passport Index as four nations tighten entry rules, reducing visa-free destinations to 55.
body:
• Iran, Bolivia, Cape Verde and Nicaragua have all ended visa-free or visa-on-arrival access for Indian passport holders in 2026
  • India's Henley Passport Index ranking has slipped to 81st from 75th, with visa-free access now at 55 destinations, down from 57
  • Iran suspended its visa waiver in November 2025 after a rise in trafficking cases where Indians were lured with false job promises
  • India has also raised passport fees for the first time in 14 years, with standard passports now costing ₹2,500

Spontaneous international trips from India just got a little harder. Four countries — Iran, Bolivia, Cape Verde and Nicaragua — have revised their entry requirements in 2026, ending visa-free or visa-on-arrival facilities for Indian passport holders and adding fresh paperwork to what were once relatively simple border crossings.

Iran: Trafficking Concerns Behind the Change

Iran's decision was the most significant. Tehran suspended its visa waiver programme for ordinary Indian passport holders effective November 22, 2025, after the Ministry of External Affairs flagged a rise in trafficking incidents. Indian nationals were being lured to Iran with false promises of employment or assured transit to third countries, only to be kidnapped for ransom upon arrival.

"The requirement now applies to both entry and transit — Indians can no longer pass through Iranian airports without a visa."

"These individuals were tricked into journeying to Iran by taking advantage of the visa waiver facility," the MEA said in a statement, advising all Indian nationals to remain vigilant and avoid agents offering visa-free travel via Iran. The requirement now applies to both entry and transit — Indians can no longer pass through Iranian airports without a visa.

Bolivia, Cape Verde, Nicaragua Follow Suit

Bolivia has replaced its visa-on-arrival service with an e-Visa requirement for all Indian nationals, effective 2026. Cape Verde and Nicaragua have similarly tightened their entry policies, though both now offer streamlined digital visa applications that are faster than traditional consular submissions.

The cumulative effect has been a modest but measurable decline in India's global passport ranking. The latest Henley Passport Index places India at 81st, down from 75th in the February 2026 edition. Indian passport holders now have visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to 55 destinations, compared with 57 a year ago.

Where Indians Can Still Travel Easily

Despite the setbacks, Indian travellers retain visa-free access to destinations across Southeast Asia, the Caribbean and parts of Africa. Countries offering visa-free entry include Thailand, Malaysia, Mauritius, Bhutan, Nepal, the Philippines, Fiji, Kazakhstan, Barbados, Jamaica and Rwanda. Visa-on-arrival facilities remain available in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Cambodia, Qatar, Jordan and Mongolia, among others.

Three destinations — Kenya, Seychelles and Saint Kitts and Nevis — require an Electronic Travel Authorization, a digital pre-approval that is typically faster than a traditional visa application.

Higher Passport Fees Add to the Picture

India has also revised passport fees for the first time in 14 years. A standard 36-page passport now costs ₹2,500, up from ₹1,500 — a 67 percent increase that applies to new applications and renewals alike.

For NRIs and frequent travellers, the message is straightforward: check visa requirements before booking, especially for destinations that were once hassle-free. The era of truly spontaneous international travel on an Indian passport is narrowing, even as digital visa systems make the added bureaucracy more manageable than it once was.
